title: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition) · Units 13–14
description: Advanced language for strong desires, joyful reactions, conflict management, antipathy, negative attitudes and distress, with usage patterns, connotations and British register.
sourceNotice: Prepared for personal study using the user-provided Cambridge book to establish learning targets. The Brazilian Portuguese translations, notes and sample sentences are original; textbook passages and exercises are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Complete Unit 13 and Unit 14 teaching sections, language-help notes and vocabulary families; exercises 13.1–13.5 and 14.1–14.5; corresponding answer-key entries for 13.1–13.4 and 14.1–14.4.
audit.pronunciation: Broad British IPA is included for short targets where confidently established. For longer multiword targets and uncertain phonetic variants, IPA is blank; connected speech is not fabricated.
audit.languagePolicy: All learner-facing English fields and metadata are in English; Brazilian Portuguese is restricted to pt fields.
audit.reviewMethod: Checked teaching text, tables and language-help boxes against facing exercises and answer-key solutions; reviewed semantic contrasts, verb patterns, intensifiers and adjective -ed/-ing distinctions. Examples and explanations are original; JSON/schema, IDs, item targets and audio-field checks performed in code. Browser import and actual TTS were not tested.
audit.limitations: No recorded MP3s are bundled. Browser import, TTS playback and pronunciation recognition require verification in the VocabLab application. Some expressions are strongly informal or British and are labelled in their notes.

units.title: Unit 13 — Emotions and reactions
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition); printed pages 32–33 (PDF pages 34–35).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition)
units.category: People and relationships · strong desires, emotional reactions, elation
learningObjectives: Recognise and express intense desires with suitable verb patterns.
Differentiate defuse, placate, conciliate and appease by purpose and register.
Describe intense happiness precisely, including formal and informal expressions.
Apply idiomatic collocations and avoid literal translations.

sectionsChecked: B · Reacting to other people’s emotions

items.pt: desejar intensamente; sentir muita vontade de
items.example: After the long hike, she craved a proper meal.
items.note: Crave is stronger than want and often takes food, attention or other strongly desired things.

items.pt: ter um desejo intenso por; estar com muita vontade de
items.example: During the stressful week, he had a craving for chocolate.
items.note: Common noun pattern: have a craving for something; often associated with food.

items.example: Her craving for recognition shaped many of her decisions.
items.note: The noun can refer to a strong desire for food or something less tangible.

items.example: The trainee showed a genuine thirst for knowledge during the workshops.
items.note: Figurative use of thirst to signal a very strong desire to learn.

items.pt: ter sede de; ter um grande desejo por
items.example: He has a thirst for adventure that keeps him travelling.
items.note: Figurative noun construction; follow for with the desired thing.

items.pt: ansiar intensamente por; ter sede de
items.example: After years in exile, the crowd thirsted for justice.
items.note: Thirst can be a figurative verb: thirst for knowledge, power or revenge.

items.example: She yearned to spend more time with her family.
items.note: Yearn expresses deep, sometimes unfulfilled longing; use yearn to do or yearn for.

items.pt: ansiar por; sentir profunda saudade de
items.example: Years later, he still yearned for the freedom of his student days.
items.note: Pattern: yearn for a person, place or experience; often something distant or unattainable.

items.example: They yearned to return home once the conflict ended.
items.note: Follow yearn with a to-infinitive when the desire concerns an action.

items.example: He had a yearning for the quiet life he had left behind.
items.note: Yearning is the noun corresponding to yearn; for introduces its object.

items.example: A sense of yearning ran through her account of childhood.
items.note: More sustained and emotional than an everyday wish.

items.example: Several firms coveted the contract because of its prestige.
items.note: Covet strongly suggests wanting to possess something desired by others; often literary or formal.

items.example: She finally secured a coveted place on the research programme.
items.note: Adjective for an opportunity, award or possession that many people want.

items.example: The fellowship became a coveted prize among young researchers.
items.note: Coveted is frequently used with prize, award, position and title.

items.pt: reduzir a tensão; apaziguar um clima tenso
items.section: B · Reacting to other people’s emotions
items.example: A short break helped defuse tension during the negotiations.
items.note: Defuse implies stopping a tense situation from becoming more dangerous.

items.pt: desarmar uma situação; acalmar um conflito
items.section: B · Reacting to other people’s emotions
items.example: The mediator used humour to defuse a potentially explosive situation.
items.note: Typically used for an escalating conflict, not simply for cheering someone up.

items.section: B · Reacting to other people’s emotions
items.example: She tried to defuse the argument before it turned personal.
items.note: Unlike diffuse (spread), defuse means remove danger or tension.

items.section: B · Reacting to other people’s emotions
items.example: The manager tried to placate disappointed customers with a prompt explanation.
items.note: Placate focuses on reducing the anger of a person or group.

items.section: B · Reacting to other people’s emotions
items.example: A sincere apology may placate someone who feels ignored.
items.note: The object is normally the angry person; distinguish this from defusing a tense situation.

items.section: B · Reacting to other people’s emotions
items.example: A respected community leader was asked to conciliate between the two groups.
items.note: Formal verb for easing conflict by dealing fairly with opposing sides.

items.pt: mediar entre duas partes em conflito
items.section: B · Reacting to other people’s emotions
items.example: The chair agreed to conciliate between two sides unable to reach an agreement.
items.note: Conciliate is formal; mediate between is often more natural in everyday professional English.

items.pt: apaziguar cedendo a exigências; fazer concessões para acalmar
items.section: B · Reacting to other people’s emotions
items.example: The board refused to appease the critics by abandoning the project.
items.note: Often disapproving: someone is made less hostile by granting demands.

items.pt: apaziguar um adversário por meio de concessões
items.section: B · Reacting to other people’s emotions
items.example: The administration offered concessions to appease its opponents.
items.note: Unlike placate, appease can imply unwarranted concessions or moral compromise.

items.pt: implacável; que não pode ser convencido a mudar
items.section: B · Reacting to other people’s emotions
items.example: Despite repeated appeals, the committee remained implacable.
items.note: Describes an opinion, hostility or stance that cannot be softened; the book warns against using placable.

items.section: B · Reacting to other people’s emotions
items.example: Decades later, implacable hatred still divided the rival factions.
items.note: A strong collocation with implacable, expressing enduring hostility.

items.section: B · Reacting to other people’s emotions
items.example: The politician described the compromise as unacceptable appeasement.
items.note: Noun related to appease; can carry disapproval in political debate.

items.example: The researchers were exultant when their experiment finally succeeded.
items.note: Fairly formal; often a response to a triumph or success.

items.example: The team arrived at the ceremony in an exultant mood.
items.note: A common pairing for happiness connected with success.

items.example: He was ecstatic when he heard he had won the scholarship.
items.note: Very strong happiness; generally more conversational than exultant.

items.example: Residents rejoiced when the missing hikers were found safe.
items.note: Relatively formal; often rejoice at or rejoice in good news or a positive event.

items.example: The families rejoiced at the announcement of the ceasefire.
items.note: At usually introduces the event or news causing joy.

items.example: Jubilant supporters gathered outside the stadium after the final.
items.note: Formal or journalistic; often describes public displays of joy after a victory.

items.pt: felicidade plena; estado de perfeita alegria
items.example: A quiet afternoon by the lake felt like pure bliss.
items.note: Noun for perfect happiness; frequently strengthened by utter or sheer.

items.example: A week without urgent emails sounded like utter bliss.
items.note: Utter is a fixed intensifier frequently used with bliss.

items.example: After months of preparation, a full weekend off was sheer bliss.
items.note: Sheer bliss and utter bliss are close alternatives.

items.pt: pleno de felicidade; em estado de bem-estar
items.example: They enjoyed a few blissful days away from the city.
items.note: Adjective derived from bliss.

items.example: The couple seemed blissfully happy in their new home.
items.note: The adverb blissfully can intensify positive states.

items.pt: completamente alheio; sem a menor ideia
items.example: The visitors were blissfully unaware of the delay at the airport.
items.note: Often ironic: the lack of awareness is pleasant only because the person does not know about a problem.

items.pt: felizmente alheio; completamente ignorante sobre um problema
items.example: He remained blissfully ignorant of the costs until the bill arrived.
items.note: A common ironic collocation; ignorant here means not informed, not necessarily foolish.

items.word: full of the joys of spring
items.pt: radiante; cheio de alegria e energia
items.example: You seem full of the joys of spring this morning; what happened?
items.note: Informal idiom, often playful, for an unusually cheerful mood.

items.example: Her parents were thrilled to bits by the graduation news.
items.note: Informal British expression for extreme happiness.

items.pt: no auge da felicidade; nas nuvens
items.example: After finishing her first marathon, Mia felt on top of the world.
items.note: Informal idiom meaning extremely happy and confident.

items.example: He has been walking on air since receiving the award.
items.note: Informal idiom for lasting elation after good news.

items.example: She was floating on air after the concert went so well.
items.note: Alternative to walking on air; often used with be or feel.

items.example: They were over the moon when their application was accepted.
items.note: Especially common in British informal English; normally be over the moon.

units.title: Unit 14 — Negative feelings
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition); printed pages 34–35 (PDF pages 36–37).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition)
units.category: People and relationships · aversion, contempt, connotation, extreme distress
learningObjectives: Distinguish antipathy, aversion, loathing and other degrees of dislike.
Use noun, verb and adjective forms for negative emotions accurately.
Interpret strongly critical adjectives according to register and connotation.
Differentiate disappointed, distressed, alarmed, devastated and distraught.

sectionsChecked: B · Language help: -ing and -ed emotion adjectives

items.example: His antipathy to unnecessary bureaucracy was well known.
items.note: Stronger and more active than simply disliking someone or something.

items.example: Public antipathy towards the proposal intensified after the debate.
items.note: Antipathy is commonly followed by towards or to.

items.example: She developed an aversion to loud crowded places.
items.note: Can refer to the dislike itself or the thing causing that dislike.

items.example: He has an aversion to public speaking despite his expertise.
items.note: To is a preposition here: use a noun or -ing form after it.

items.pt: sentir aversão por; sentir repulsa a
items.example: I immediately felt an aversion to the proposed arrangement.
items.note: Alternative to have an aversion to; indicates strong reluctance or dislike.

items.pt: algo que a pessoa detesta especialmente
items.example: Pointless meetings are her pet aversion at work.
items.note: A personally recurring strong dislike; similar in use to pet hate.

items.example: He is averse to taking unnecessary risks.
items.note: Adjective: be averse to something or doing something; not followed by a bare infinitive.

items.pt: não ser contrário a; até gostar de
items.example: I am not averse to changing my mind when the evidence is strong.
items.note: A conventional understatement often implying openness or mild enthusiasm.

items.example: She spoke with unmistakable loathing about the fraudulent scheme.
items.note: Noun for exceptionally strong hatred or disgust.

items.example: He loathes being treated as though he cannot make decisions.
items.note: Stronger than dislike; commonly takes a noun or an -ing clause.

items.example: They exposed the loathsome exploitation behind the operation.
items.note: Describes a person, action or practice that provokes intense disgust.

items.example: Her abhorrence of cruelty shaped the organisation’s policies.
items.note: Usually used for an intense moral disgust; commonly abhorrence of.

items.example: The committee abhors the use of violence against civilians.
items.note: Formal and strong verb often used about morally objectionable behaviour.

items.example: The witnesses called the discriminatory treatment abhorrent.
items.note: Frequently describes something regarded as morally shocking.

items.example: The proposal was met with scorn by many local residents.
items.note: Both noun and verb; implies contempt and lack of respect, not just irritation.

items.example: She gave a scornful reply to the suggestion.
items.note: Scornful describes a person, remark or tone expressing contempt.

items.example: He has always been scornful of superficial publicity campaigns.
items.note: The book’s exercises reinforce scornful of versus the verb scorn without of.

items.example: His repeated interruptions caused considerable irritation.
items.note: A moderate negative reaction, weaker than loathing or abhorrence.

items.example: The constant notifications irritated everyone in the office.
items.note: The verb names the cause of someone’s annoyance.

items.example: The high-pitched sound was increasingly irritating.
items.note: The -ing adjective refers to what causes the feeling.

items.example: I felt irritated when the same question was asked repeatedly.
items.note: The -ed adjective describes the person experiencing the feeling.

items.example: The sudden announcement caused distress among the staff.
items.note: Noun or verb for severe worry or upset; stronger than ordinary annoyance.

items.example: The documentary contained several distressing accounts.
items.note: The -ing form describes news or events that cause emotional pain.

items.example: She was visibly distressed after the difficult phone call.
items.note: The -ed form describes the person affected.

items.example: The unusual movement of the structure caused alarm among the engineers.
items.note: As a feeling, alarm means strong worry or fear; the word can also be a verb.

items.example: The inspection revealed an alarming rise in defects.
items.note: Describes information or events that cause concern or fear.

items.example: Residents were alarmed by the sudden evacuation order.
items.note: The -ed adjective describes those experiencing fear or concern.

items.example: The supervisor sounded offhand when responding to the intern’s concerns.
items.note: Suggests an impolite lack of interest or consideration; not simply relaxed.

items.pt: tratar alguém com indiferença ou grosseria
items.example: The receptionist was offhand with several visitors.
items.note: Characteristic pattern: be offhand with somebody.

items.pt: intrometido; autoritário por excesso de zelo
items.example: An officious attendant insisted on checking every minor detail.
items.note: Disapproving: someone is too eager to enforce rules or direct others.

items.example: Their ostentatious decorations attracted unwanted attention.
items.note: Suggests showy displays intended to impress, especially of money or status.

items.example: The company attracted criticism for its ostentatious display of wealth.
items.note: Strong collocation; often carries a negative judgement.

items.example: His pompous introduction made a routine meeting sound historic.
items.note: Criticises exaggerated self-importance or unnecessary formality.

items.example: The restaurant’s pretentious menu put some customers off.
items.note: Implies trying too hard to appear sophisticated or important.

items.example: The debate descended into puerile jokes instead of addressing the issue.
items.note: Formal, strongly critical term for childish or silly behaviour by someone expected to be mature.

items.example: Sloppy record-keeping undermined the reliability of the results.
items.note: Informal and disapproving, especially of careless work or appearance.

items.example: Her fickle support for the team disappeared as soon as it began losing.
items.note: Describes repeatedly changing loyalties, opinions or preferences.

items.pt: implicante com detalhes mínimos; excessivamente minucioso
items.example: The team found the reviewer’s nit-picking comments unhelpful.
items.note: Informal, negative attention to trivial faults; hyphenated adjective.

items.example: An obnoxious passenger shouted at the train staff.
items.note: Strongly critical of rudeness or offensiveness.

items.example: The candidate felt dejected after several unsuccessful interviews.
items.note: Typically disappointed after failure or rejection.

items.example: She was utterly dejected when her proposal was rejected.
items.note: Utterly intensifies extreme disappointment.

items.example: A forlorn figure waited alone outside the closed station.
items.note: Implies loneliness, sadness and lack of support.

items.example: The family were devastated by the sudden loss of their home.
items.note: Extremely upset or shocked by serious bad news; not merely disappointed.

items.example: The team were utterly devastated by the unexpected tragedy.
items.note: The adverb underscores severe emotional impact.

items.example: The distraught parents waited for news of their missing child.
items.note: Very upset and worried, sometimes too distressed to think calmly.

items.example: I have been feeling down since the project was cancelled.
items.note: Informal mood adjective; milder than devastated or distraught.

items.example: She felt down after returning from a wonderful holiday.
items.note: Everyday informal pattern for temporary sadness.

items.example: He looked miserable throughout the long, lonely winter.
items.note: Conveys great unhappiness and can also describe an unpleasant experience.
